An API is like a messenger that lets two different pieces of software talk to each other without needing to know how the other one works inside.

Imagine you’re at a restaurant. You don’t walk into the kitchen and cook your own meal. Instead, you tell the waiter what you want from the menu. The waiter takes your order to the kitchen, and then brings back your food. You never need to know how the kitchen is organized or how the chef prepares the dish — you just get what you asked for.

An API works the same way. One program (like a weather app on your phone) wants something from another program (like a big weather data service). The app “tells” the API what it needs (for example, “give me today’s temperature for New York”), and the API carries that request to the other system, then brings back the answer. The app doesn’t have to understand the complicated inner workings of the weather service — it just uses the simple menu the API provides.

So, an API is basically a set of rules and a messenger that lets software ask for information or actions from other software in a predictable, easy way.
